# Neural, convolutional, and graph decoders {#sec-neural-graph}

A neural decoder's architecture encodes assumptions about physics. A dense network assumes every input may interact immediately with every hidden unit. A convolution assumes repeated local structure. A recurrent network assumes a repeated temporal update. A graph network assumes that interactions should follow a specified connectivity. These choices influence sample efficiency, extrapolation, memory traffic, and latency as much as parameter count does.

The aim of this chapter is to derive the principal constructions and identify what each can and cannot guarantee. We distinguish a model's output interface, the topology over which it computes, and the decision rule applied to its outputs. These three choices are often conflated under the name of an architecture.

## Two decoding interfaces {#sec-neural-interfaces}

A **low-level decoder** predicts a physical correction. In one binary CSS sector, it maps $s$ to $\hat e\in\mathbb F_2^n$ and must satisfy $H\hat e=s$. A **high-level decoder** starts with a reference correction $T(s)$ and predicts its residual logical class. This guarantees a well-defined recovery after combining the predicted class with the reference, provided $T(s)$ was constructed correctly.

For one logical qubit, high-level classification has four classes, independent of the number of physical qubits. For many logical qubits, the joint class space grows as $4^k$; the apparent simplicity is then lost. A neural correction generator has a larger output but may be easier to combine with local streaming or sliding-window procedures. A global logical-outcome classifier may be highly accurate for an entire memory experiment and still lack the interface needed for intermediate corrections or a logical computation.

Varsamopoulos, Criger, and Bertels demonstrated feedforward classification for small surface codes [@varsamopoulos2018feedforward] ([primary paper](https://doi.org/10.1088/2058-9565/aa955a)). Their work helped establish the usefulness of reducing recovery to logical classification. Krastanov and Jiang developed a probabilistic neural stabilizer decoder [@krastanov2017probabilistic] ([primary paper](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41598-017-11266-1)). These are foundational demonstrations, with their performance claims tied to the tested small codes and noise assumptions. They do not establish an architecture-independent asymptotic neural threshold.

A high-level network trained relative to a particular $T(s)$ learns that convention. Replacing the reference decoder without relabeling data changes the meaning of every output. Let $T'(s)=T(s)\overline L_{a(s)}G(s)$. The new class is $l'=l\oplus a(s)$ in binary logical coordinates. This transformation must be applied consistently to training labels, inference outputs, and logical-observable definitions.

## Dense networks: useful baselines with a scaling cost {#sec-neural-dense}

Flatten $m$ syndrome bits into $x\in\mathbb R^m$, use hidden width $h$, and output $K$ class logits. A one-hidden-layer network requires approximately $mh+hK$ weights and corresponding multiply-accumulate operations. The forward pass has a fixed operation count for a fixed input size, a valuable contrast with variable-iteration search. That does not make it constant time as $m$ grows, nor does it imply fixed latency on finite hardware.

Dense models are useful when the code is small, boundaries dominate geometry, or one wants a transparent baseline. Their weakness is that the network must learn repeated local rules independently at many positions. Changing distance changes input dimension, and ordinarily requires changing parameters. Padding can allow shared dimensions, but does not by itself teach how boundaries or logical strings transform with size.

A lookup-table decoder can also be viewed as a function approximator. Its table has up to $2^m$ entries. A neural model compresses the mapping only if useful regularity exists in the syndrome distribution. Universal approximation results concern representability on a fixed input domain; they do not promise a compact representation, efficient training, or robust behavior on unseen syndromes.

Chamberland and Ronagh studied deep decoders within circuit-level fault-tolerant protocols, including surface-code, Steane, and Knill constructions [@chamberland2018deep] ([primary preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.06441)). The enduring methodological lesson is to include the entire error-correction circuit in training and to evaluate runtime alongside accuracy. An input distribution generated by ideal parity measurements misses propagated hook errors and faulty ancilla operations.

### Learning targets across code families

Maskara, Kubica, and Jochym-O'Connor systematically compared versatile feedforward decoding on topological codes with different noise structures [@maskara2019versatile] ([primary paper](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevA.99.052351)). This highlights a useful distinction: reusing a decoding formulation across codes is easier than reusing a trained weight vector. Davaasuren, Suzuki, Fujii, and Koashi analyzed constructions and target representations for accurate learned decoders, including finite-data considerations and spatially informed architectures [@davaasuren2020framework] ([primary paper](https://doi.org/10.1103/PhysRevResearch.2.033399)). Their work motivates choosing a label representation that preserves the logical information relevant to recovery before increasing network capacity.

## Convolution and spatial locality {#sec-neural-convolution}

For a regular two-dimensional syndrome array $x_{i,j,c}$, a convolution computes

$$
h_{i,j,a}=\phi\!\left(b_a+\sum_{\Delta i,\Delta j,c}W_{\Delta i,\Delta j,c,a}x_{i+\Delta i,j+\Delta j,c}\right).
$$ {#eq-neural-convolution}

The indices $c$ and $a$ label input and output channels. The same kernel $W$ is used at every lattice position. A translation of the input translates the output, apart from boundary effects. This **equivariance** is an exact property of the construction under matching padding and geometry; it reduces the number of independent rules to learn.

For a kernel of side $r$, $C$ input channels and $D$ output channels, the parameter count is $r^2CD$, independent of lattice area, while computation is proportional to the number of sites. After $L$ stride-one layers, a feature depends only on sites within a radius proportional to $L(r-1)$. This region is its receptive field.

Local noise often creates local clusters, so a small receptive field handles many common events efficiently. However, two defects separated by a distance much larger than the receptive field cannot directly influence each other's local output. Logical ambiguity can depend on an extended path to a boundary or around a torus. Increasing width at fixed depth does not enlarge that region. Solutions include multiscale pooling, dilation, repeated local updates, a global logical head, or a conventional decoder for remaining defects.

The distinction is physical. A fixed-radius local rule can be effective for typical small error clusters below threshold while failing on rare extended clusters. Whether those failures decay sufficiently with distance is a separate question. In higher-dimensional codes, local correction has different possibilities than in two-dimensional surface codes. Breuckmann and Ni exploited this structure in convolutional decoding of higher-dimensional toric codes [@breuckmann2018neural] ([primary paper](https://quantum-journal.org/papers/q-2018-05-24-68/)). Their numerical results should not be transferred to a two-dimensional circuit-level surface-code setting.

A complementary route uses renormalization-inspired hierarchy: infer local information, coarse-grain it, and repeat at progressively larger scales. Ni's large-distance toric-code decoder follows this strategy [@ni2020large] ([primary paper](https://quantum-journal.org/papers/q-2020-08-24-310/)). Hierarchy provides a mechanism for extending receptive fields with depth; its success remains dependent on training and the noise model. Gicev, Hollenberg, and Usman combine convolution, boundary information, and a residual cleanup decoder for differently shaped large surface codes [@gicev2023scalable] ([primary paper](https://quantum-journal.org/papers/q-2023-07-12-1058/)). Their work separates the scalability of local neural processing from the remaining global inference task. A theoretical parallel implementation should still be distinguished from a measured complete hardware controller.

### Boundaries and channels are physical information

A surface-code image should identify check type, missing checks, boundary type, and potentially data-qubit locations. Filling absent checks with zero conflates "not measured here" with "measured without a detection event." A separate mask removes this ambiguity. A toric lattice uses periodic geometry; planar zero padding silently changes that topology.

The $X$ and $Z$ sectors can be separate channels. Under depolarizing noise, $Y$ errors correlate the sectors. A network receiving both can exploit those correlations. A fair baseline should include a correlated conventional decoder when available. Beating an independent-sector baseline may demonstrate the value of correlation information rather than a unique advantage of neural approximation.

## Recurrence and syndrome histories {#sec-neural-recurrence}

A noisy check measurement cannot be interpreted from one round alone. If $m_{a,t}$ is the measured check bit, a detection event is often $d_{a,t}=m_{a,t}\oplus m_{a,t-1}$, with separately defined initial and final boundaries. A recurrent model updates a hidden state,

$$
h_t=F_\theta(h_{t-1},d_t),\qquad q_t=G_\theta(h_t).
$$

The same $F_\theta$ is used every round. This shares temporal rules and permits arbitrary sequence lengths. It also creates a compression problem: $h_t$ must retain the past information needed to interpret future observations.

A simple recurrence $h_t=\tanh(Wh_{t-1}+Ud_t+b)$ can have vanishing or exploding gradients. The derivative across many rounds contains a product of Jacobians. If typical singular values are below one, long-range training signals shrink; above one, they grow. A long short-term memory network introduces a cell $c_t$ and gates,

$$
\begin{aligned}
f_t&=\sigma(W_f[d_t,h_{t-1}]+b_f),&
i_t&=\sigma(W_i[d_t,h_{t-1}]+b_i),\\
g_t&=\tanh(W_g[d_t,h_{t-1}]+b_g),&
o_t&=\sigma(W_o[d_t,h_{t-1}]+b_o),\\
c_t&=f_t\odot c_{t-1}+i_t\odot g_t,&
h_t&=o_t\odot\tanh c_t.
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-neural-lstm}

The additive cell update creates a path by which information can persist when $f_t\approx1$ and $i_t\approx0$. Gates decide what to forget, write, and expose. This alleviates a training problem; it does not guarantee indefinite perfect memory.

Baireuther, O'Brien, Tarasinski, and Beenakker used recurrent networks to exploit temporal and correlated error information in topological-code decoding [@baireuther2018correlated] ([primary paper](https://quantum-journal.org/papers/q-2018-01-29-48/)). The recurrent viewpoint is a bridge between early neural decoders and modern recurrent Transformers. Its important scaling distinction is fixed hidden memory per spatial code size as experiment duration grows.

For color codes, Baireuther, Caio, Criger, Beenakker, and O'Brien incorporated flag-qubit information in a recurrent decoder under circuit-level noise [@baireuther2019color] ([primary paper](https://doi.org/10.1088/1367-2630/aaf29e)). A flag is an extra measurement designed to reveal otherwise dangerous propagated faults. Feeding flags to the network can preserve distinctions that the ordinary syndrome discards. The example reinforces a general principle: better observations and better inference are separate resources. A network cannot recover information never recorded by the extraction circuit.

To train recurrence, unroll $T$ updates and apply backpropagation through the resulting computation graph. Full training stores activations for all $T$ rounds. Truncated backpropagation limits the gradient horizon and memory cost; it may leave the model weak on correlations longer than that horizon. Testing on long durations is therefore essential even when recurrence formally accepts any duration.

A final-readout head can use terminal data measurements. A streaming head cannot. Report which head produces the quoted result, whether hidden states reset between experiments, and whether training examples share overlapping histories.

## Graph neural networks from first principles {#sec-neural-gnn}

A graph has vertices and edges. A Tanner graph is bipartite: variable vertices represent error components or faults, and check vertices represent parity constraints. An edge connects variable $i$ to check $a$ when $H_{ai}=1$. For a general stabilizer representation, edge labels can record whether a qubit participates through $X$, $Y$, or $Z$. For circuit-level detector models, fault variables connect to every detector they flip, possibly producing hyperedges.

Belief propagation already computes on this graph using local messages. A graph neural network replaces or supplements its analytic update rules with trainable functions. One construction maintains variable states $h_i^{(t)}$ and check states $g_a^{(t)}$:

$$
\begin{aligned}
m_{i\to a}^{(t)}&=M_v(h_i^{(t)},g_a^{(t)},u_{ia}),\\
g_a^{(t+1)}&=U_c\!\left(g_a^{(t)},s_a,\sum_{i\in N(a)}m_{i\to a}^{(t)}\right),\\
n_{a\to i}^{(t)}&=M_c(g_a^{(t+1)},h_i^{(t)},u_{ia}),\\
h_i^{(t+1)}&=U_v\!\left(h_i^{(t)},\lambda_i,\sum_{a\in N(i)}n_{a\to i}^{(t)}\right).
\end{aligned}
$$ {#eq-neural-message-passing}

Here $u_{ia}$ is an edge feature and $\lambda_i$ is a noise prior, such as a log-likelihood ratio. Sum aggregation is invariant to neighbor ordering. Shared update functions make the algorithm equivariant under graph relabeling: relabeling vertices consistently relabels outputs. Mean or attention-weighted aggregation is also possible, but degree information may need an explicit feature.

For bounded degree, hidden width $h$, and $T$ iterations, a typical implementation costs $O(T|E|h^2)$, where $|E|$ is edge count. This is linear in block length only when degree, width, and iteration count remain fixed. If preserving accuracy requires growing $T$, the effective scaling changes. Sparse graph operations can also be memory-bound and slower on a particular accelerator than denser, better-optimized kernels despite fewer arithmetic operations.

### BP as a special design anchor

For binary parity checks, BP passes variable-to-check log-likelihood ratios

$$
L_{i\to a}=\lambda_i+\sum_{b\in N(i)\setminus a}L_{b\to i},
$$

and check-to-variable messages

$$
L_{a\to i}=2\operatorname{atanh}\!\left[(-1)^{s_a}\prod_{j\in N(a)\setminus i}\tanh(L_{j\to a}/2)\right].
$$

The syndrome sign enforces whether the parity should be even or odd. A learned version can rescale messages, alter damping, choose a schedule, or inject a GNN update between BP runs. This retains a physics-informed starting point while using data to correct repeated-message correlations and trapping behavior.

Gong, Cammerer, and Renes studied GNN updates between BP stages for quantum LDPC decoding [@gong2024gnn] ([primary institutional record](https://doi.org/10.1109/ISIT57864.2024.10619589)). Ninkovic and collaborators developed graph-message-passing quantum LDPC decoders [@ninkovic2024gnn] ([primary preprint](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.05170)). Maan and Paler's Astra demonstrates learned Tanner-graph updates and distance extrapolation in numerical benchmarks [@maan2025astra] ([primary paper](https://doi.org/10.1038/s41534-025-01033-w)). These works motivate learned local inference, but their reported comparisons apply to their code families, noise models, iteration settings, and baseline implementations.

Graph structure makes cross-size execution possible without resizing every matrix. It does not establish successful zero-shot decoding of arbitrary code families. Two graphs may have different degree distributions, cycles, trapping sets, logical rates, or noise correlations. Transfer must be measured, and a successful parity solution must still be evaluated for logical correctness.

## Degeneracy-aware training and exact constraints {#sec-neural-constraints}

Suppose a physical-output network predicts independent bit probabilities $q_i$. Binary cross-entropy against the sampled error favors that particular representative. A soft parity term can enforce approximate consistency. Under the model's independent Bernoulli distribution,

$$
\Pr_\theta\!\left(\bigoplus_{i\in N(a)}e_i=s_a\right)
=\frac{1+(-1)^{s_a}\prod_{i\in N(a)}(1-2q_i)}{2}.
$$ {#eq-neural-soft-parity}

To derive it, note that $(-1)^{\oplus_i e_i}=\prod_i(-1)^{e_i}$ and $\mathbb E[(-1)^{e_i}]=1-2q_i$; independence factorizes the expectation. Taking the negative log of this expression gives a differentiable consistency penalty.

This expression is exact for the factorized model, not for a correlated physical posterior. Multiplying these check probabilities does not produce the true joint probability of satisfying all checks, because checks can overlap. Moreover, a low soft penalty does not ensure that independently thresholded bits satisfy any check. Verify the discrete result or use an exact repair step.

An alternative guarantees consistency algebraically. Solve $He_0=s$ and find a basis $K$ of $\ker H$. Then every valid correction is $e=e_0+Ku$ over $\mathbb F_2$. A network predicts $u$, and any output satisfies the syndrome. This parameterization includes both stabilizer and logical directions; it does not automatically select the correct coset. A separate logical loss or class probability is still needed.

For quantum codes, logical-class losses are naturally invariant under stabilizers. When using a physical target, one can minimize or sum over equivalent representatives, but doing so exactly may be as hard as the original inference. A hybrid practical choice is to predict class information or improved priors and retain a reliable conventional solver for exact constraints.

## Symmetry beyond weight sharing {#sec-neural-symmetry}

A transformation $g$ is a symmetry of a decoding task only if it preserves the code, observation rule, noise distribution, and cost, with known action on labels. A square-lattice rotation may exchange boundary types and logical $X/Z$ roles. A spatial translation is exact on an ideal torus but generally not on a calibrated planar device. Rotating a syndrome while leaving anisotropic gate error rates unchanged is not a symmetry of that device.

Data augmentation adds transformed examples $(g\cdot s,g\cdot l)$. Equivariant architectures enforce the transformation law structurally. Ensemble averaging can define

$$
\bar q(l\mid s)=\frac1{|G|}\sum_{g\in G}q(g\cdot l\mid g\cdot s)
$$

for a finite symmetry group with consistent conventions. This reduces sensitivity to arbitrary representation choices but multiplies inference cost. If symmetries change the reference correction, label transformations must include the induced logical shift.

A different invariance is gauge freedom under stabilizer multiplication: two error representatives have the same physical action on encoded states. This is not a spatial symmetry. A model can be spatially equivariant and still use an inappropriate nondegenerate target. Both structures must be addressed.

## A small Julia demonstration of learned message passing {#sec-neural-julia}

The following code illustrates one check update and differentiable parity calculation without any ML package. It is deliberately small enough to inspect. The graph is the three-bit repetition graph; the syndrome is $10$, and prior bit-flip probability is $0.1$.

```julia
H = [1 1 0; 0 1 1]
s = [1, 0]
p = 0.1
prior = fill(log((1-p)/p), 3)
check_to_var = zeros(2, 3)
for a in 1:2, i in 1:3
    H[a, i] == 0 && continue
    others = [j for j in 1:3 if H[a, j] == 1 && j != i]
    product = prod(tanh(prior[j]/2) for j in others)
    check_to_var[a, i] = 2atanh(clamp((-1)^s[a] * product,
                                     -1 + 1e-12, 1 - 1e-12))
end
posterior_llr = prior + vec(sum(check_to_var, dims=1))
q = 1 ./ (1 .+ exp.(posterior_llr))
soft_satisfaction = [
    (1 + (-1)^s[a] * prod(1-2q[i] for i in 1:3 if H[a,i] == 1))/2
    for a in 1:2
]
println("Bit probabilities after one update: ", q)
println("Soft check probabilities: ", soft_satisfaction)
```

In a neural BP experiment, replace the final sum by $\lambda_i+\sum_a w_{ai}L_{a\to i}$ and fit $w$ on training samples. Compare shared weights, edge-specific weights, and weights shared across iterations. The first encourages transfer and uses fewer parameters; the second can absorb device inhomogeneity; the third trades iteration-specific flexibility for reuse. A useful experiment measures logical failure, discrete constraint violations, and runtime together.

## Exercises {#sec-neural-exercises}

1. **Reference-correction covariance.** Two reference corrections differ by a logical $X$ on a single-logical-qubit code. How should a four-class network's outputs transform?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Worked solution

Ignoring phase, multiply every logical label by $X$: $I\leftrightarrow X$ and $Z\leftrightarrow Y$. The probability vector is permuted accordingly. This is a change of class convention, not a change in physical noise. Using the old probabilities with the new reference would produce a systematic logical mistake.
:::

2. **Graph radius.** An update alternates variable-to-check and check-to-variable messages. How far can information travel after $T$ complete updates? Does fixed $T$ imply successful decoding at arbitrary distance?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Worked solution

One complete update moves information across two Tanner-graph edges, so a variable depends on a radius at most $2T$ in that graph. Fixed $T$ gives a finite receptive field even when the graph grows. It may decode typical local clusters, but cannot directly compare arbitrary distant patterns. Successful extrapolation requires evidence about which clusters dominate failure and whether a global head, repeated processing, or fallback handles them.
:::

3. **Soft parity versus hard recovery.** Let one even-parity check touch three bits with predicted probabilities $q=(0.49,0.49,0.99)$. Calculate the soft satisfaction probability and test the hard decision.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Worked solution

The product is $(0.02)(0.02)(-0.98)=-0.000392$. Even-parity probability is $0.499804$. Thresholding at $1/2$ gives $001$, which has odd parity and violates the check. Differentiable expectations do not replace checking the final discrete correction.
:::

4. **Compute scaling.** A bounded-degree graph has $n$ variables, fixed hidden width $h$, and $T=n^{1/2}$ iterations. What happens to a claimed linear-time decoder?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Worked solution

With $|E|=O(n)$ and fixed $h$, work scales as $O(Tn)=O(n^{3/2})$. Each iteration is linear, but the complete algorithm is not. Parallel depth is also at least proportional to $T$ when iterations depend sequentially on earlier messages. Hardware parallelism can reduce time within an iteration, subject to bandwidth and communication limits.
:::
